source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs (NeurIPS 2024), full PDF v3
finding: The 38.1% headline is a relative gain, not percentage points. It is the mean of per-cell relative improvements of UoT over direct prompting. I re-computed it from Table 1 and it reproduces the paper's own Llama3-70B figure exactly.
numbers: Table 1, 5 datasets x open/closed set. Llama3-70B: mean per-cell relative gain 46.6% (paper text says 46.6%); same cells average +10.1 absolute points. Mistral-Large 46.3% rel / +9.4 pts. Gemini-1.5-Pro 44.6% / +12.8. Claude-3-Opus 23.1% / +9.2. Implied GPT-4 about 29.9% rel (derived from 5x38.1 minus the other four; GPT-4 rows are garbled in the PDF text). Ratio-of-means would give 28.8% for Llama, so the metric is the mean of cell ratios. Paper text: FloDial GPT-4 43.7 to 67.3 (+23.6 pts).
quote: UoT enhances the success rate by 38.1% compared to DP across 5 datasets and 5 different LLMs
limits: The paper never defines the metric; this is my reconstruction. GPT-4 rows not machine-readable. All answers come from a GPT-4 simulator. The abstract-level number is easily misread as +38 points.
agent_relevance: Quote UoT as roughly +10 points absolute (about +30-45% relative) on its benchmarks, not +38 points. Closes the definition part of gap 10.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts, Table 2 (equal-token comparison) and open-set rows of Table 1
finding: Only paper in the set with a token-matched comparison. At about 4.5-4.7k GPT-4 tokens per game, pruned UoT beats Adapted-ToT and CoT-SC. At about 9.2-9.3k tokens, UoT beats Adapted-ToT with extra depth. Gains also hold in the open-set variant where the hypothesis list is not given.
numbers: Table 2 (20Q / Medical Dx / Troubleshooting, GPT-4, closed set): CoT-SC k=33 at 4.6k tokens 32.6/37.6/42.5; Original-ToT D=3 4.5k 23.7/65.3/40.4; Adapted-ToT D=3 4.5k 33.8/85.1/60.3; Pruned UoT D=3 4.7k 48.1/88.4/63.2; Adapted-ToT D=4 9.3k 40.9/86.7/63.7; UoT D=3 9.2k 54.4/92.5/66.0. Open-set vs closed-set gain over direct prompting (4 LLMs x 5 datasets = 20 cells each, my computation from Table 1): open set +9.8 points (47.3% rel), closed set +10.9 points (33.0% rel); UoT below or equal to DP in 0 of 40 cells.
limits: Baselines are tree search with LLM self-scored reward, not plain long reasoning. GPT-4 is a non-reasoning model. No o-series or thinking-model arm. Open set means the LLM lists its own possibilities, but the first three 20Q rounds use direct prompting and the answerer is a GPT-4 simulator that sees the true answer.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gaps 1 and 2: structured uncertainty scoring beats other ways of spending the same tokens for a non-reasoning model, and the gain survives an open hypothesis set. It says nothing about a reasoning model given the same tokens.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts, Appendix E (simulation depth)
finding: One-step lookahead already gets most of the gain; deeper lookahead adds more on diagnosis and 20 Questions than on troubleshooting.
numbers: Figure in App. E read from the PDF text (series are interleaved, so assignment to datasets is my best reading, consistent with the final depth-3 values in Table 2): Medical Dx 82.6 -> 86.7 -> 92.5 at depth 1/2/3; Troubleshooting 66.1 -> 67 -> 67.3; 20 Questions 63.5 -> 64.7 -> 75.2. Depth 1 reaches about 89% (MD), 98% (TB), 84% (20Q) of the depth-3 score.
limits: Figure values, not a table; dataset assignment inferred. 20Q here uses Common and BIG-bench sets. LLM-simulated lookahead, not exact computation. Only to depth 3 for budget reasons.
agent_relevance: Gives a number for gap 9 on the LLM side: one step captures roughly 85-98% of a three-step plan, so one-step scoring is a sound default.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (MAI-DxO), Section 3.2 design
finding: There is no component ablation. The five variants differ in cost control and ensembling, not in which role is present. The panel is one model role-playing five personas, so the roles cannot be separated with the paper's data.
numbers: Panel roles: Dr. Hypothesis (top-3 probability-ranked differential, Bayesian-style updates), Dr. Test-Chooser (up to 3 tests that discriminate between leading hypotheses), Dr. Challenger (devil's advocate, proposes tests that could falsify the leader), Dr. Stewardship (cheaper equivalents, veto low-yield tests), Dr. Checklist (validity). Variants: Instant Answer, Question Only, Budgeted, Unconstrained Budget, Ensemble. Author statement: variants selectively enable or disable capabilities.
limits: Test choice is by LLM judgement, not computed information gain. Evidence for Challenger and Hypothesis is qualitative (hand-inspected disagreements with off-the-shelf o3).
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open: the cost saving cannot be assigned to a role. Best available split is panel vs budget tracker vs ensemble (see d05).

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models, results and appendix A
finding: Against a reasoning-model baseline (o3), the plain panel gives a small accuracy gain and a large cost cut. A separate budget tracker cuts cost further at a small accuracy loss. Ensembling buys accuracy at about the baseline cost. On o3 and o4-mini the accuracy gain was not statistically significant; the cost cut was.
numbers: NEJM sequential benchmark, 304 cases (56 test). o3 baseline 78.6% at $7,850. MAI-DxO no budget 81.9% at $4,735 (cost -39.7%, accuracy +3.3 pts). Budgeted config 79.9% at $2,396 (text elsewhere says $2,397), cost -69.5% vs baseline. Ensemble 85.5% at $7,184. Physicians 19.9% at $2,963 (56 cases, 764 diagnoses). Average gain across off-the-shelf models about 11 pts. Single vs batched testing ablation on test set: both 83.9%, cost $3,991 single vs $5,084 batched. Permutation test p<0.005 for gains except o3/o4-mini accuracy.
limits: The 56-case test set scores higher than the 304-case set. Costs are estimated test prices. Panel-vs-no-panel is confounded with prompt format, since the baseline uses a uniform simple prompt. The Gatekeeper is an LLM.
agent_relevance: For a reasoning model the scaffold mostly saved money (-40% by panel alone), with at most a modest accuracy gain. Partial answer to gap 3 and gap 4. The batch ablation says fewer, single probes did not hurt accuracy and cost less.

source: Li et al. (2024) MediQ: Question-Asking LLMs and a Benchmark for Reliable Interactive Clinical Reasoning (NeurIPS 2024), full PDF
finding: Asking by default hurts. The tested fix is a separate confidence check before each turn: rate confidence 1-5 with a written rationale, repeated 3 times, and ask only below a threshold. The best variant beat the ask-always setup and the no-ask setup, but still closed only half the gap to full information.
numbers: BASIC (model may ask) averages an 11.3% relative accuracy drop vs no-question Initial across LLMs; most samples get zero questions asked (Fig 5). Best abstention (Scale + rationale generation + self-consistency 3) beats BASIC by 22.3% and Initial by 12.1%, and closes 51.2% of the gap between Initial and Full. Plain self-consistency without rationale degrades performance. Thresholds were grid-searched per setting (App. D). Cleaning repeated and unanswerable questions plus paragraph format gave +5.7 pp over BASIC (+2.3 over Initial). Models above 70B beat Initial with the best abstention; smaller ones did not. Rationale lowered expected calibration error from 0.286 to 0.211.
limits: Percentages in the paper are not always labelled relative or absolute. Threshold tuned on the evaluation data. Patient simulator is an LLM reading a fixed record. Sample size per dataset not re-checked here.
agent_relevance: A measured trigger exists: verbal confidence with a rationale, thresholded. It is fragile (tuned threshold; self-consistency alone hurts). Gap 5 partly closed; see d07 and d08 for non-medical triggers.

source: Edwards and Schuster (2026) Ask or Assume? Uncertainty-Aware Clarification-Seeking in Coding Agents
finding: In coding, having the same agent decide when to ask works poorly. Splitting out a separate binary 'is this underspecified' checker that forces the next action to be a user query recovers nearly full performance and asks only when needed. A forced-ask baseline asks nearly always.
numbers: Underspecified SWE-bench Verified, 500 tasks, 100 iterations, permutation tests. Claude Sonnet 4.5 resolve rates: Full spec 70.8; Hidden (no asking possible) 54.8; Interactive baseline (told to ask) 70.4; single-agent self-detect 61.2; two-agent with Intent Agent 69.4 (p<0.001 vs single; p=0.621 vs Interactive; p=0.458 vs Full). Kimi K2.6: 69.4 two-agent vs 61.6 single; Interactive baseline only 47.2 because of tool-misuse failures. Queried 344 of 500 tasks; where it did not ask it resolved 76.9% (Hidden on the same tasks 77.6%); where it asked 66.0% (Hidden 44.5%). Queries per task 3.06 (two-agent) vs 1.84 (single). Ask rate rose 9.28 pts from easy to medium tasks (two-agent) vs 2.43 (single). Kimi two-agent asked 8.71 times per task, poorly calibrated.
limits: Simulated user with the true issue. Clarification is about missing facts, not about picking the most informative test. Two frontier models only. Cost of the extra agent not reported in the main text.
agent_relevance: Best non-medical evidence for gap 5: a separate, cheap gate on 'should I ask' beats self-judged asking, and asks less on easy tasks. Supports a schema gate before probing, kept apart from the solver.

source: Dong et al. (2026) Value of Information: A Framework for Human-Agent Communication
finding: Asking when the expected utility gain exceeds the cost of asking matches or beats tuned confidence thresholds and fixed question counts in most settings, with no tuning, but not at high question cost. Cost-aware asking measured on four domains.
numbers: GPT-4.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash; 20Q, medical diagnosis (terminal utility 10 for correct), flight preference, ambiguous WebShop. Mixed 20Q at cost c=0.01 with GPT-4: VoI utility 14.14 vs best tuned confidence threshold 11.49 (theta=0.90). Gemini Mixed 20Q Table 1 (VoI minus best of 4 baselines x 9 settings): c=0.01 +0.34; 0.02 +0.84; 0.05 +1.36; 0.10 -0.90; 0.20 -0.96 (best baseline there is not asking at all). Thresholds are sensitive: best theta varies with cost.
limits: The headline 'up to 1.36 points' omits the two losses at high cost. Probabilities inside VoI come from LLM predictions; no calibration guarantee. Costs are user-effort numbers chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to cost-weighted probing with a measured outcome outside medicine, though it prices questions to a user rather than probes to an environment. Gap 6 stays mostly open; gap 5 gets a second trigger design.

source: Pedrozo, Soares, de Oliveira (2026) Do Reasoning Models Ask Better Questions? Information-Theoretic Analysis on Multi-Turn LLM Games
finding: Models with explicit reasoning get more information per question when they cannot see the hypothesis space, but even then they pick the best of their own candidate questions only about a fifth to a third of the time. Thinking raises the quality of the candidate set, but selection is poor.
numbers: Guess My City, 40 targets x 3 runs = 120 games per model, max 30 turns, Qwen3 as oracle/pruner. Partially observable: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct (no thinking) win rate 0.10, 29.13 turns, 0.14 bits per turn; Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking win 0.93, 14.88 turns, 0.42 bits. Qwen3-8B no CoT win 0.08, 29.60 turns; with CoT clearly higher (row partly unreadable). Llama-3.1-8B no CoT win 0.81. Fully observable: all about 1.00 win; Thinking 7.12 turns vs Instruct 7.95. Share of turns where the thinking model chose the max-IG candidate among those it considered: 0.26 (30B, fully obs), 0.25 (30B, partial), 0.36 (8B, full), 0.19 (8B, partial); 7.63 candidates per turn (30B partial) and 9.74 (8B).
limits: Instruct vs Thinking are different checkpoints, so thinking is confounded with training. Binary questions over a tree of cities. Only Qwen/Llama; no o-series. Candidates were parsed from reasoning traces by another LLM. Single workshop-style paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: reasoning models improve but leave headroom a code-side scorer could take. They list several candidates and then choose the maximum-information one rarely. Argues for 'let the model generate, let code select'.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench: Can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks? (Google DeepMind)
finding: Asking the right single question is hard for LLMs, including reasoning models, on logic and planning, and chain of thought or few-shot examples did not help much. A plain breadth-first search over the constraint structure solves it, so a computed rule beats model judgment.
numbers: Multiple-choice: choose the minimal question. GPT-4o, o1-preview, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking Exp, Gemma 2; zero-shot, CoT, 4-shot. Best models saturate GSM-Q and GSME-Q but score only about 40-50% on Logic-Q and Planning-Q (abstract). BFS baseline on Logic-Q: depth 3 39.0%, depth 5 80.6%, depth 10 99.8%. Models can solve the fully specified version yet fail to pick the question. Gemini 2.5 Pro traces appear only as qualitative examples (App. E).
limits: Table 2 rows are interleaved in the PDF text, so I did not assign per-model scores. Single missing variable, no cost, no noise. Experiments done 06/2024-03/2025; newer reasoning models were not scored.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: reasoning models are not good at choosing what to ask; search over the problem structure is. Supports computing the probe from an explicit model of the problem where one can be built.

source: Kirichenko et al. (2025) AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions (abstract via arXiv API only)
finding: Reasoning fine-tuning reduces the tendency to abstain on unanswerable or underspecified questions, which would work against any 'know when to ask' trigger in a reasoning model.
numbers: 20 datasets, 20 frontier LLMs. Reasoning fine-tuning degrades abstention by 24% on average, even in math and science. A careful system prompt boosts abstention but does not fix it.
limits: Abstract only; full text not opened, so the 24% metric and its base are unchecked. Abstention is not the same as asking a probe.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 5: do not assume a reasoning model will notice when it should probe. Put the 'should I probe' check in the scaffold.

source: Su and Cardie (2026) Knowing but Not Showing: LLMs Recognize Ambiguity but Rarely Ask Clarifying Questions
finding: Models can label a query ambiguous when asked directly, but in ordinary answering they almost never ask. Adding retrieved context makes them even less likely to ask.
numbers: 10 models (6 OpenAI, 2 Claude 3.5, 2 Qwen2.5). In the QA setting clarifying-question rates reach only about 5% on ambiguous questions in the best case (without context) and fall further with context. With retrieved context, ambiguous-question QA accuracy rises 46% to 55% for the group discussed; smaller models gain 15-30 pts, frontier models 2-8 pts; top models 70%+ on unambiguous vs about 60% on ambiguous with context. gpt-5 is the response-type judge.
limits: Static ambiguity, not a diagnostic search. Judge-model labels. Only non-reasoning chat models from 2024-2025.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: recognition is not the problem; acting on it is. The scaffold should turn an uncertainty flag into a forced probe step instead of relying on the model to volunteer it.

source: Chari and Pattanaik (2026) Wild Guesses and Mild Guesses in Active Concept Learning
finding: With an open hypothesis space proposed by an LLM, picking the max-information query can hurt. It chooses boundary cases that wipe out the particles, the LLM then proposes invalid or over-specific hypotheses, and learning stalls (a 'support-mismatch trap'). A positive-test strategy is faster on easy rules but fails to falsify on medium rules, where EIG wins.
numbers: Number Game on 0-100, Gemini 2.5 Flash as proposal engine, max 50 queries, convergence at 0.95 posterior on the top hypothesis. Queries to convergence (EIG / PTS / random), cleanly readable cells: Square numbers 3/2/2; Odd numbers 7/4/2; Even <30 17/31/17; Digits sum <8 43/DNF/DNF; Remainder 5 mod 9 31/DNF/41. Several other cells interleave in the PDF text and are not used. Authors: query choice cannot fix a generator that gives the target little mass.
limits: Workshop-style, single run per cell, about 12 rules. The 'PTS' is a positive test on the top hypothesis, i.e. confirmation-style, not a deliberate falsification probe.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 8: EIG is not safe when hypotheses are LLM-proposed and open. Suggests a meta-policy: cheap safe probes first, switch to falsifying, high-information probes when progress stalls or contradictions appear (authors' untested proposal).

source: Marozzo and Lio (2026) LLM-as-an-Investigator: Evidence-First Agentic Reasoning for Robust Interactive Problem Diagnosis
finding: Troubleshooting with technical forum threads (non-medical). A component ablation exists, with a counterfactual role that challenges the leading hypothesis and picks discriminating questions. Removing it costs about 5 points; removing follow-up questions costs about 4; thinking mode alone did nothing.
numbers: 303 threads, 100 cases evaluated, Gemini backbone. Final score /100: Baseline 67.3, Thinking (no questions) 67.5, Thinking + interaction 72.8, Ask-5 72.3, ReAct 69.0, ToT 61.5, full SIA 79.2 (CI 72.7-83.7) with 9.0 hypotheses and 5.2 questions. Ablations (final/potential): no structured investigation 72.8/84.7; no counterfactual critique 74.0/85.5; no weight updates 78.5/88.5; no hypothesis expansion 76.5/79.3; no follow-up questions 75.0/85.0; no final adjudication 76.0/89.2. Other backbones: SIA minus Thinking+interaction = +6.2 and +7.7. Misleading-user stress test, 10 paired cases: final 80.0 vs 76.0, wrong suggested cause selected in 2/10.
limits: Simulated user answers from forum text. Overlapping CIs on several comparisons; ablations on the same 100 cases with no repeat intervals; stress test only 10 cases. The counterfactual role is not a computed information-gain scorer.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 8 outside medicine: a challenger-style probe and real follow-up questions each add several points; extra thinking without interaction added nothing. Gap 1 hint: questions beat thinking at similar question counts.

source: Qiu, Li, Su, Chen (2025) Interactive Text-to-SQL via Expected Information Gain for Disambiguation
finding: Ranking clarification questions by expected information gain over sampled SQL candidates beats raw information gain, most-probable-first and random orderings, but by modest margins on execution accuracy. The simulated user always answers correctly.
numbers: Spider ambiguous subset (top candidate confidence below 0.7), N=290 questions. Execution accuracy: EIG 76.6% vs Info Gain (uniform prior) 73.4% vs Max Probability 72.1% vs Random 70.1%. Exact match: EIG 38.3% vs Info Gain 21.0% vs Max Probability 19.0%. Hard questions, exact match: 40.2% vs Random 6.6% and Min-Prob 8.0%.
limits: Authors list noisy or wrong user answers as future work, so noise robustness is untested. Preprint; artifact link is a placeholder. Subset built by the model's own confidence.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: shows a non-game task with a model-built candidate set, positive but small gains in execution accuracy (+6.5 over random) and no test of unreliable answers.

source: Choudhury et al. (2025) BED-LLM (ICLR 2026), targeted re-read for noise, mismatch, cost and Implicit Maximization
finding: The paper tests answerer mismatch (a different model answers than the one that reasons) and a soft free-text preference task. It also ran an LLM-picks-from-samples arm and reports wall-clock. Gains hold under mismatch and shrink on the soft task. Letting the model choose among the sampled candidates is cheaper and helps, but 'works much less well' than computed EIG.
numbers: Film-preference task: 200 user profiles in free text, answerer rates films 1-5 in 0.5 steps, 5 questions; Prompt-Only is a stronger baseline there than on 20 Questions and BED-LLM gives a boost 'most clear' when questioner and answerer are different model classes (figure only, no table). 20Q cross-model setups (e.g. questioner GPT-4o-mini, answerer Qwen2.5-72B) keep the benefit. Wall-clock for 20Q on the Animals set, Qwen2.5-72B: Data-Estimation 1 day 17 h; BED-LLM about 2.5 h; Implicit Maximization about 45 min; CoT about 35 min; Prompt-Only about 26 min (row order inferred). Ranking of 5 candidate questions at 10 sampled hypotheses already matches that at 85.
limits: Wall-clock is not token-matched and the method rows are interleaved in the PDF text. No reasoning-model questioner. Answerer noise is cross-model, not random or wrong answers; wrong-answer injection is not tested. The free-text task has no accuracy metric of the target, only a judge rating.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: computed EIG costs about 6x the wall-clock of Prompt-Only; no arm gives plain reasoning 6x compute. Gap 2: gain survives model mismatch, weakens on the soft free-text task.

source: Hutson et al. (2025) GuessingGame: Measuring the Informativeness of Open-Ended Questions in LLMs
finding: In a fully open-ended game with free-form questions and no candidate list, information gain (scored after the fact with an LLM) predicts how fast the game ends. Free prompt-only constraints that stop repeated question types raised success a lot with no extra compute.
numbers: 858 games. LLaMA-3.3 70B success 39.4% standard; with repeat-constraint 80.0%; with forced open-ended questions 97.4%. GPT-4o 64.1% standard vs 98.5% forced-open; Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite 74.1% vs 87.3%. One standard deviation more Bayesian IG cuts expected game length 43% (entropy-based IG 19%). Open-ended prompts beat yes/no: 39.4% vs 32.1%. The same IG metric correlates with efficiency in human play (Spearman -0.95 experts, -0.90 naive).
limits: The large gain comes because the baseline fell into enumerative questioning; the answerer is an LLM. IG is estimated with LLM-scored relevance so it is noisy. Not a controlled test of computed selection.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2: cheap structural rules on probe form (no repeated type, open-ended allowed) beat the untouched baseline by more than computed scoring did on other tasks. Test these first, since they cost no extra tokens.

source: de Kleer (1991) Focusing on Probable Diagnoses (AAAI-91)
finding: States why GDE's minimum-entropy probe choice uses only one step: with a very large number of diagnoses, multistep lookahead is too costly. When only a handful of leading diagnoses are kept, this paper does full lookahead instead. It has no head-to-head numbers on one-step versus deeper lookahead.
numbers: Focused ATMS keeps about 5 leading diagnoses for the n-bit adder (which has 3n-1 minimal diagnoses); the unfocused implementation exceeds 60 s at about 50 components, the focused one is roughly linear to about 1500. Leaf cost of the decision tree is the log of the candidate's posterior probability. Tie-break: pick the probe nearest a possibly faulty component.
limits: This is a speed and design paper, not a probe-count comparison. Original GDE (1987), de Kleer 1992 and the 2006 papers were not obtainable (paywalled; scholarly APIs returned 429), so gap 9 is not closed. Focusing can propose probes far from the true fault.
agent_relevance: Confirms the design choice: cheap one-step entropy over a small set of leading hypotheses, with a locality tie-break. Also a warning: probes chosen on a truncated hypothesis set can be bad.

source: Breese and Heckerman (1996) Decision-Theoretic Troubleshooting: A Framework for Repair and Experiment (UAI)
finding: Under single fault, independent components and fixed costs, the minimum expected-cost sequence is ordered by probability divided by cost, and it needs no decision tree. The system uses cost estimates myopically and replans after each step. In their printer example the best pure repair sequence was about as good as the best non-base observation.
numbers: Printer network example: pure repair sequence expected cost 13.62 min; best non-base observation then repair 13.71 min; best configuration-observation plan 12.98 min total (10.98 plus 2 for setting the configuration). Probabilities come from a Bayesian network. Earlier simulation (Heckerman et al. 1995, cited): the decision-theoretic troubleshooter had lower expected repair cost than a static cost-based procedure, also with multiple faults.
limits: Needs the stated assumptions (single fault, independent costs, limited observations). Numbers are from a Windows 95 printing model, not a modern LLM setting. The earlier simulation figures are cited, not reread.
agent_relevance: Gaps 6 and 7: p/c ordering is a proven rule where its assumptions hold, and the priors come from a model of the device. For an LLM agent, rank by belief over cost as a check, but the belief inputs must come from somewhere.

source: Golovin and Krause (2011) Adaptive Submodularity: Theory and Applications in Active Learning and Stochastic Optimization (JAIR)
finding: Greedy adaptive selection is provably within a logarithmic factor of the best policy for pool-based active learning with noise-free answers, but the strong bound was corrected after publication.
numbers: Greedy policy for adaptive stochastic minimum cost coverage: average cost at most the optimal times (ln(Q/delta)+1)^2 in general and (ln Q + 1)^2 for self-certifying instances. Earlier versions claimed a single log factor; a flaw was found by Nan and Saligrama (2017), and whether the single-log bound holds is listed as open. Feige hardness: no better than ln Q approximation unless NP is in DTIME(n^O(log log n)).
limits: Noise-free outcomes. Existing claim K13 says 'near optimal'; read it as 'log-factor competitive in the worst case, often close in practice'. Theory gives no practical percentages.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 (theory side): one-step greedy is the principled default with a worst-case guarantee; it does not say how much deeper lookahead gains on real diagnosis tasks.

source: Amin (2026) Bayesian Orchestration of Multi-LLM Agents for Cost-Aware Sequential Decision-Making (single-author preprint)
finding: Only LLM study found that ablates the prior. On synthetic resume screening, empirical class priors cut misclassifications versus uniform priors. It also prices information-gathering with value of information. Low trust: synthetic data and model-made labels.
numbers: 1,000 synthetic resumes labelled by GPT-4o, 5 LLMs. Empirical prior [0.65, 0.25, 0.08, 0.02] gave 176 misclassifications vs 387 with a uniform prior. Reported total cost down $294,000 (34%) vs best single LLM; cost units: hire error $40,000, wasted interview $2,500, phone screen $150. Ablation shares reported as multi-LLM aggregation 51%, sequential updating 43%, disagreement-triggered information gathering 20% (these sum above 100%, so they overlap or are inconsistent).
limits: Synthetic data, generated labels, one unaffiliated author, no repeated runs, no real deployment. Not a diagnosis task and no probe-order test. Treat as a hint only.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: priors mattered in this one test, and they were set from known base rates, not from the LLM. No evidence yet that GDE-style failure-rate priors help an LLM debugging agent.

source: Coburn, Sanner, Silver (2026) Social Chain of Thought: multi-agent differential diagnosis (best-of-n compute control)
finding: On static differential diagnosis (no probing), repeated sampling of one model with up to 35 draws did not match a structured multi-agent pipeline in recall and lost precision. A rare compute-matched control, but not for probe selection.
numbers: Open-XDDx, 570 cases, Qwen-2.5-32B. Baseline recall 0.531, precision 0.472, F1 0.493. Best-of-35 recall 0.537, precision 0.403, F1 0.454 (text-confirmed); adding a judge brought recall to 0.499. Authors report the multi-agent recall gain across models as four to twelve points.
limits: Table rows are interleaved in the PDF text; I use only values the running text confirms. Different task (differential list, no tests). The structured pipeline uses more calls than the baseline, so only the best-of-n arm is compute-matched.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: where compute-matching was done at all, structure beat plain repeated sampling. This is not about choosing probes, so gap 1 for probe selection stays open.
